newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - MGAM under pressure as redemptions mount.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - MGAM under pressure as redemptions mount.

text.p: Morgan Grenfell came under pressure on Tuesday to confirm it has a contingency plan in place to cover further withdrawals from its beleaguered investment funds as redemptions continued.

But Morgan Grenfell Asset management, the fund management arm of German banking giant Deutsche Bank AG, took some comfort from the fact that Tuesday's redemptions amounted to some 24 million stg, down from Monday's 39 million.

But the new figure moved the total to just over 250 million stg and ever nearer exhausting the 300 million stg pile of cash the firm has in place to cover withdrawals following last week's temporary suspension of the funds.

The suspension followed the disclosure that there had been irregularities in the way they have been run and led to two fund managers being suspended and a full-scale regulatory investigation being launched.

In Frankfurt, Deutsche shares closed 39 pfennigs lower at 71.50 marks, above earlier lows, with sentiment hit by news the bank's precious triple-A credit rating was under examination by Moody's Investor Service, one of the most influential debt rating organisations in the market.

Banking analysts continued to cut their 1996 earnings forecasts for Deutsche with Konrad Becker at Merck, Finck pruning his estimate to 4.5 marks from 5.0, but maintaining his buy recommendation on the stock.

In London, Morgan Grenfell would neither confirm nor deny the existence of a plan to raise extra cash, but industry sources said the money is likely to be in place already to satisfy regulators that continuing investor demand for redemptions will be met.
"It's inconceivable that Deutsche hasn't made a plan just in case they need to top up the amount of money they have available," said one senior source.

The current 300 million stg cushion is made up of the 180 million stg Deutsche pumped into the funds last week by removing some of the unlisted stocks, which were the original cause of the problems and cash, which was already present.
MGAM has three options available to raise further cash.
There could be another plain injection of money by Deutsche, which would probably be the simplest way out but might have wider repercussions for the German banking giant.

MGAM could also sell some of the contents of the funds, but this could be painful given the lack of liquidity in some of the investments and the fact that, as a distressed seller, MGAM's market competitors will play hard ball.

The final alternative looks the most likely. With permission from fund trustees, Royal Bank of Scotland, MGAM would be able to borrow 10 percent of the value of the funds from its wealthy parent to finance redemptions.
It is likely that Deutsche would prefer this route because it could be paid back from the fund when the dust has settled.

The bank's previous 180 million stg injection has not disappeared down a black hole but it is almost impossible to estimate what the securities, which have a high proportion of speculative high-tech unlisted stocks, will be worth when they have been properly valued.
Meanwhile, an investigation by industry watchdog the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) continues and is likely to do so for well over a month.

The Securities and Investments Board, whose rules regulate the investment management industry, is also said to be planning a complete review of the regulations governing the running of funds to see if similar situations can be avoided.

In the meantime, independent financial advisors, who deal daily with small scale investors wanting to make their private nest-eggs grow, have been flooded with calls from people wanting reassurance about the safety of their investments following the Morgan Grenfell debacle.
